title: When the Bell Breaks
premise: Felix Almeida, a property surveyor who has spent his life making himself unnoticeable, is hired to appraise his late grandmother's house and finds it cataloguing him back: every photograph now contains an extra chair, and the house hums a song he half-remembers from childhood. The house belongs to something that collects the overlooked, and Felix's lifelong invisibility has marked him as its next resident. To survive, he must learn the song's final verse—the one that names the collector—without singing along, because joining the chorus means surrendering his identity forever. In the end, Felix sings the verse aloud as a naming rather than an offering, binding the entity to the house's walls and choosing, for the first time, to be seen by walking out the front door into daylight.
about_author: Rosalind Ravensworth is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate sales in coastal New England, where she developed a professional unease about houses that seem to remember their occupants. She writes horror about belonging, bureaucracy, and the quiet violence of being unnoticed.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Arriving at his grandmother's derelict house to appraise it for probate, Felix measures rooms that return slightly different numbers each time. He keeps his routine—lights on, doors counted—and tells himself the drafts explain everything. Emotional beat: uneasy competence masking loneliness; the reader learns Felix survives by being unremarkable.

chapters.title: An Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV Felix. Sorting photographs for the estate inventory, Felix notices every family picture now includes one more chair than it should—an empty seat angled toward the camera. His childhood photos have changed too. He photographs the photographs; the copies show nine chairs. Emotional beat: dread arrives through domestic detail; his invisibility suddenly feels like bait.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: POV Felix, with a brief interlude in grandma's 1974 journal. The house gains a door overnight—a thin one, painted the color of a throat. The journal mentions 'the verse' and warns never to hum along when the walls sing at night. Felix realizes grandma spent fifty years not singing. Emotional beat: inherited vigilance; grief curdling into fear.

chapters.title: The Surveyor Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: POV Marisol, Felix's colleague sent to assist. She can't remember his face by lunchtime, misfiles his reports under 'vacant,' and finds his name already struck from the firm's roster. When she confronts him, he thanks her for noticing—the first person in years who has. Emotional beat: the cost of invisibility made literal; fragile human connection.

chapters.title: Verse One
chapters.summary: POV Felix. At 3 a.m. the house sings—a lullaby in no language he knows, and Felix catches himself mouthing along before biting his tongue bloody. In the mirror, his reflection sits in the extra chair. He researches the melody and finds it matches a sea shanty from the drowned village the house was moved from. Emotional beat: the trap tightening; identity as contested territory.

chapters.title: What the House Collects
chapters.summary: POV Felix and journal fragments interleaved. In the cellar he finds the previous residents: coats on hooks, shoes by size, names embroidered inside collars—all people history forgot. Grandma's journal reveals she bought her survival by feeding it her sister. Emotional beat: horror of complicity; Felix understands the price of survival is always someone else.

chapters.title: Marisol Comes Back
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Refusing to accept the paperwork, Marisol drives to the house and nearly walks into the thin door, which opens onto her own childhood kitchen. Felix pulls her back, and together they map the house's logic: it lures each person with what they long for. Emotional beat: alliance formed; belonging offered by a person instead of a predator.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Felix. The house stops pretending: walls breathe, chairs rearrange into an audience, and the song reaches its penultimate line, leaving silence where the last verse should be. Grandma's ghost—or memory—shows him where she hid the ending: written backward in the ledger, because naming the collector is the only power the collected keep. Emotional beat: revelation and resolve; knowledge as inheritance.

chapters.title: Sing Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Felix, climax. The house floods with the chorus, every hooked coat swaying, and the collector—vast, patient, shaped like an empty chair—offers Felix a seat and total peace. He recites the final verse as a naming, not a hymn, speaking the entity's true name without melody. The house convulses; the thin door slams to ash. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into defiance; identity claimed at the brink.

chapters.title: Seen
chapters.summary: POV Felix, coda with a Marisol epilogue beat. Weeks later, the house stands ordinary and empty; the appraisal lists it honestly. Felix signs his full name on the report, lets Marisol introduce him to her friends, and keeps one photograph—the one with ten chairs—as a reminder. The last image: somewhere, another house begins to hum. Emotional beat: hard-won belonging; survival's price acknowledged but refused.
